result: The manuscript identifies a critical gap in cell type nomenclature: while single-cell RNA-sequencing has led to an explosion of cell type definitions (C1), there is no widely followed standard convention for naming brain cell types (C29), resulting in widely varying nomenclature and limited alignment between taxonomies (C2). Despite the existence of several public databases for data storage (C31), a community-recognized repository for storing and tracking cell type assignments does not currently exist (C32).
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C29, C30, C31, and C32 collectively establish the problem that the CCN aims to address. These claims are supported by citations to published work and represent accurate characterizations of the current state of the field. The claims are internally consistent and provide clear motivation for the development of the CCN.

result: The Allen Institute created the Common Cell Type Nomenclature (CCN) for matching and tracking cell types across studies (C3), which is qualitatively similar to gene transcript management across different genome builds (C4, C35). The CCN can be readily applied to new or established taxonomies (C5) and was applied to diverse cell type datasets derived from multiple quantifiable modalities (C6). The CCN was motivated by methodologies from GENCODE and HGNC (C35, C36) and an initial version was introduced in October 2019 (C37).
evaluation: Claims C3-C6 and C35-C38 describe the creation and motivation of the CCN. These claims are well-supported by the manuscript content, citations to relevant prior work (GENCODE, HGNC), and demonstration of application to multiple datasets. The analogy to gene nomenclature systems is appropriate and well-justified.

result: The CCN schema is built on two core concepts: (1) a taxonomy, defined as the output of a computational algorithm applied to a specific dataset (C39), and (2) a cell set, which can represent any collection of cells within a specific taxonomy (C40). Provisional cell types are quantitatively derived data clusters (C41) that can be organized hierarchically or non-hierarchically (C42). The CCN assigns unique identifier tags to taxonomies and cell sets (C43, C45, C46), along with multiple types of aliases (C47, C48) and metadata tags (C50, C51, C52).
evaluation: Claims C39-C52 describe the technical structure of the CCN system. These claims are well-supported by the manuscript text, figures (particularly Figure 1), and Table 1. The definitions are clear, internally consistent, and the system is demonstrated through application examples. The use of UBERON ontology (C52) is appropriately cited.

result: The CCN is currently in use by the Allen Cell Types Database for transcriptomic taxonomies (C53) and is being applied to taxonomies generated by the BRAIN Initiative Cell Census Network (BICCN) (C54). User-friendly executable code for applying the CCN is available on GitHub (C55).
evaluation: Claims C53-C55 describe the current implementation and availability of the CCN. These claims are directly supported by the manuscript text, citations to BICCN publications, and provision of a GitHub repository link. The claims demonstrate practical utility and community adoption of the system.

result: The CCN utilizes a strategy for naming cell types in the mammalian cortex based on properties that are cell intrinsic and potentially well conserved between species (C56). For glutamatergic neurons, cell types are named based on predominant cortical layer localization and predicted projection patterns (C57-C62). For GABAergic interneurons, developmental origin defines cell types by their canonical marker gene profile (C63-C65).
evaluation: Claims C56-C65 describe the specific naming convention for mammalian cortical cell types. These claims are well-supported by citations to published work demonstrating laminar organization (C58-C60), cross-species conservation (C59), and developmental origins (C63-C65). The naming strategy is presented in Table 2 and is internally consistent with the broader CCN framework.

result: A reference taxonomy is defined as any taxonomy based on high-confidence datasets that can be used as a baseline for comparison (C66). The manuscript presents a cross-species M1 reference taxonomy based on nearly half a million nuclei from mouse, marmoset, and human (C69-C70), integrating data from three omics modalities (C70-C71). The integrated taxonomy identified 45 core provisional cell types aligned across all species (C75), with 11 total taxonomies generated (C73) that are largely consistent across modalities (C76).
evaluation: Claims C66-C77 describe the concept and implementation of a reference taxonomy using the M1 dataset. These claims are well-supported by citations to Bakken et al., 2020a, Figure 3, and supplementary materials. The integration of multiple species and modalities is clearly demonstrated, and the identification of 45 aligned cell types represents a concrete, quantifiable result.

result: Nuclei from human MTG were aligned to the human M1 dataset (C78), enabling biological insights such as the presence of L4-like neurons in M1 where an anatomically defined L4 is not apparent (C79), and enabling prediction of cell properties such as long-range connectivity and electrophysiology in brain regions inaccessible to techniques like Patch-seq (C80).
evaluation: Claims C78-C80 describe Use Case 1 for the CCN. C78 is supported by citation to Bakken et al., 2020a. C79 represents a specific biological insight enabled by the alignment, supported by Figure 4. C80 describes potential applications of the alignment approach. These claims demonstrate practical utility of the CCN for cross-dataset comparison.

result: A study of mouse visual cortex examined ~1800 cells characterized electrophysiologically (C81), with morphological reconstructions performed on 450 cells (C82). Using multimodal unsupervised clustering, 20 excitatory and 26 inhibitory morpho-electric types (me-types) were identified (C83).
evaluation: Claims C81-C83 describe Use Case 2, demonstrating application of the CCN to a non-transcriptomic taxonomy. These claims are supported by citation to Gouwens et al., 2019 and Figure 5. The claims accurately represent the study design and results, demonstrating that the CCN can be applied to taxonomies based on morphology and electrophysiology.

result: Somatostatin-expressing interneurons can be divided into multiple cell types, some of which express Chodl in mouse cerebral cortex (C84). These 'Sst Chodl' neurons are rare and correspond to the only known cortical interneurons with long-range projections (C85). Recent Patch-seq studies confirmed that 'Sst Chodl' cell sets characterized by morphology and electrophysiology match those defined by transcriptomic profiles (C86).
evaluation: Claims C84-C86 describe Use Case 3, demonstrating how the CCN enables tracking of a specific cell type across multiple modalities and taxonomies. These claims are well-supported by citations to published work (Tasic et al., 2018; Gouwens et al., 2020; Tomioka et al., 2005) and Table 3. The example effectively demonstrates the utility of the CCN for multimodal integration.

result: A single-cell transcriptomics study of turtle and lizard pallium found GABAergic interneuron and non-neuronal cell types to be homologous with those in mouse cortex (C87), with shared gene markers suggesting a shared evolutionary origin across 320 million years (C88). Reptilian analogs for CGE- and MGE-derived GABAergic types were identified, though VIP and PVALB marker genes are not expressed in reptiles (C89). RNA-seq identified two distinct sublayers of turtle layer 2 that seem to correspond with mammalian deep and upper layer neurons (C91).
evaluation: Claims C87-C91 describe Use Case 4, demonstrating application of the CCN to cross-species comparison between reptiles and mammals. These claims are supported by citation to Tosches et al., 2018 and Supplementary file 1. The claims accurately represent the findings and demonstrate that the CCN can be applied beyond mammalian species, though with appropriate caveats about the complexity of glutamatergic neuron homology.

result: The CCN currently lacks the centralization and governance of gene-based standards like HGNC (C92) and does not yet have a mechanism for integrating with underlying data and metadata (C93). The manuscript discusses future directions including ontology curation (C94-C95), centralized databases (C96-C97), Cell Type Cards (C98-C99), and a governing body (C100). The Allen Institute has begun combining ontology development, data integration, and nomenclature formalization efforts (C101), with a dedicated community forum for discussion (C102).
evaluation: Claims C92-C102 describe current limitations and future directions for the CCN. C92-C93 are honest assessments of current limitations. C94-C100 describe potential future developments with appropriate citations and examples (e.g., GeneCards, Yao et al., 2020b). C101-C102 describe ongoing efforts. These claims appropriately distinguish between current capabilities, limitations, and future possibilities.

result: The manuscript provides extensive background on cell type classification, including its historical importance in neuroscience (C7-C10), the impact of high-throughput methods like scRNA-seq (C11-C14), differences between retina and brain in terms of cell type correspondence (C15-C19), complications from graded properties (C20), and divergence across species and developmental/disease trajectories (C21-C24).
evaluation: Claims C7-C24 provide background context for the development of the CCN. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to published work. These claims accurately represent the state of the field and provide important context for understanding the challenges that the CCN addresses. The claims are internally consistent and well-supported by the literature.

result: The manuscript describes progress in computational alignment methods for matching cell types across datasets (C25-C26), including methods like Patch-seq (C27) and autoencoder-based dimensionality reduction (C28). The challenge of cell type nomenclature has been recognized by the community (C33) and was addressed at a Cell Type Ontology Workshop in June 2019 (C34).
evaluation: Claims C25-C28 and C33-C34 describe prior work on alignment methods and community recognition of nomenclature challenges. All claims are supported by appropriate citations to published work. C34 provides specific details about the workshop that informed the CCN development. These claims provide important context for the development of the CCN.

result: The CCN properties can be tracked using a relational graph or other database service, in a qualitatively similar manner to how transcripts are tracked across different versions of GENCODE genome builds (C44).
evaluation: Claim C44 describes the potential for tracking CCN properties using database services, drawing an analogy to GENCODE. This claim is supported by citation to Frankish et al., 2019. The claim is consistent with the overall design philosophy of the CCN and represents a reasonable technical approach, though implementation details are not provided.
